title: NexPath - Hosting decision: latency & throughput sizing scan
summary: Discovery call to size latency and throughput needs for NexPath's chat summarization product. Customer sketched 100-500 qps burst patterns, strict p95 SLAs of 1200ms for streaming, interest in dedicated pools or private VPC for data residency and KMS. Agreed next steps: baseline token/sec numbers, run short POC on dedicated pool, share security pack and pricing estimate.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-02
Start: 15:30 PT
Duration: 54 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Maya López (Redwood SE), Samir Rao (NexPath CTO), Emily Chen (Lead ML Eng), Marcus Lee (SRE)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood, joining with Maya, our solutions eng. How's everyone doing?
[00:09] Samir: Good, thanks. Sorry we're a little delayed, had a standup run long.
[00:12] Emily: Hi. Yep all good. Marcus on mute.
[00:16] Marcus: yeah sorry, sorry.
[00:18] Jordan: No worries. High level, we wanna understand p95 targets, concurrency and whether you want hosted, dedicated or private — and then map that to throughput and cost. Maya will jump into some numbers after we walk your traffic profile.
[00:30] Samir: Cool. Quick context: NexPath is building a live meeting summarization feature. We ingest a stream of transcription tokens and produce incremental summaries for user sessions. Typical sessions are 10-15 minutes, but we have spikes when multiple meetings start at the same time — like 200+ concurrent summaries during peak. We currently use a vendor-hosted API but latency and costs are too variable.
[00:54] Jordan: Got it. What's your acceptable p95?
[00:57] Emily: For interactive UX we're targeting p95 end-to-end for the summary chunk to appear under 1.2s for streaming cases. For non-streamed batched summaries it's ok to be 2.5-3s.
[01:10] Maya: Good, so 1200ms p95 streaming. And do you have a target tokens/sec per session or average length?
[01:18] Samir: Each session generates about 120 tokens / minute on average — speakers talk slow in meetings. Summaries yield about 30-80 tokens every 20-30 seconds depending on verbosity.
[01:29] Marcus: Also want to mention we need data residency in EU for several customers, and KMS integration is mandatory. SOC 2 is a must.
[01:40] Jordan: Understood on KMS and SOC2; we have a security pack. We'll share the SOC2 docs and KMS integration guide. For residency, we can route to EU-only clusters or recommend Private.
[01:50] Emily: Question: How do you handle KV cache when streaming many concurrent sessions? We found KV growth blew up memory on our side.
[01:58] Maya: Yeah good question. Our runtime supports per-session KV eviction policies and shared KV cache for identical prefixes. For streaming, we typically keep a short prefix cache and offload long histories to a shardable object store — that helps when you have many long-lived sessions. There are tradeoffs with latency for cold reads though.
[02:18] Samir: Mhmm. For baseline numbers, we're looking at both 13B and 70B model variants. We want to know token/sec throughput and p95 values for both under 200, 500, and 1000 concurrent streaming sessions.
[02:33] Maya: Okay we can approximate now and then run targeted benchmarks. As a rule of thumb, the 13B quantized path at 16-bit or int8-ish runs roughly X tokens/sec on a T4-ish vs A10-ish — sorry, I'm mixing clouds. Let me give you ballpark: 13B per-GPU sustained streaming might do 600-900 tokens/sec depending on beam size and kv handling; 70B is an order of magnitude lower per-GPU — like 80-200 tokens/sec. But concurrency is handled via multiplexing and batching.
[02:58] Emily: Those ranges are helpful but can you translate to our p95 1.2s target? For example, with 200 concurrent streaming sessions, what do we need to keep tails under 1.2s?
[03:10] Maya: Rough calc: if each session needs to produce ~50 tokens every 30s — that's ~1.7 tokens/sec per session average, but streaming p95 is dominated by per-request headroom and batching latency. For 200 sessions at 1.7 tokens/sec that's 340 tokens/sec sustained. To keep p95 under 1.2s we'd want headroom ~3-4x so aim for ~1.2k tokens/sec capacity. So for 13B that might be 2 GPUs (if each does ~600 tps sustained) with an efficient batching and small batch windows; for 70B you'd need multiple 70B instances or cheaper fallback to distilled model.
[03:44] Samir: So you're suggesting mixed routing — send most to 13B dedicated and fallback to smaller distilled or higher quantized version for bursts?
[03:52] Jordan: Exactly. We typically recommend a primary low-latency model with a cost-friendly variant for overflow and automated fallback. That keeps p95 predictable and reduces cost.
[04:01] Marcus: Any guidance on batching windows? We need low latency but also want to not waste GPU cycles.
[04:06] Maya: For streaming, we use very small batch windows (10-20ms) and continuous batching — that gives low tail latency while still coalescing tokens. For non-streaming batch summaries you can use larger windows 50-150ms and get much better throughput.
[04:22] Emily: Ok. Also curious about cold start behavior. If a new session fires on a GPU that has lots of other sessions, do you warm KV caches proactively?
[04:30] Maya: We do warm start heuristics. Also we can pin hot sessions to particular nodes for a while. In Dedicated mode you get more control — predictable capacity — whereas Hosted will auto-route and can spill to other regions if needed.
[04:42] Samir: We have multi-region failover requirements — primarily EU, with a US fallback. Does Redwood support cross-region routing with SLO-aware failover?
[04:50] Jordan: Yes, routing policies let you prefer EU, then fall back to US; you can set SLO windows and automatic fallback if p95 exceeds threshold. We can configure that as part of the POC.
[04:58] Marcus: Security follow-up: audit logs retention and who can see logs — need to ensure logs don't contain PII.
[05:05] Jordan: Our audit logs can be scrubbed, redacted, and exported to your SIEM; we also support customer-managed KMS and optional on-prem connectors for Private deployments. We'll send the security data sheet.
[05:16] Samir: Great. Can we talk cost a bit? If we go Dedicated with 2 GPUs for 13B and fallback to a distilled 6B for overflow, what's the monthly ballpark?
[05:25] Jordan: A quick rough estimate — depends on cloud type. Dedicated reserved capacity pricing starts with a base for the pool and then usage. We'll send a model-based pricing spreadsheet; we can run scenarios. For now, expect dedicated pool to be higher fixed cost but lower variable unit cost per token compared to hosted bursts.
[05:40] Maya: To make this concrete we should run a token/sec benchmark with your actual prompt shapes. We can do a short POC: 24-48 hour run that simulates 200, 500 and 1k concurrent streaming sessions and measure p95 and tail jitter. We'll run it on dedicated capacity and on hosted to compare.
[05:55] Emily: That would be ideal. Timeline: we need to decide hosting mode within 3 weeks to meet product launch.
[06:03] Jordan: Ok we'll prioritize the POC. Next, any constraints with your infra? VPC peering or private deployment?
[06:09] Marcus: We prefer a VPC/VPN peering for Dedicated. Private on-prem might be a stretch but possible for certain customers. Need SAML for SSO.
[06:18] Jordan: We support VPC peering and SAML SSO; Private on-prem packages require a little more lead time. We'll outline the lead times in the follow-up.
[06:27] Samir: Can we get the baseline numbers for ingestion token/sec? Also curious about queuing behavior — if load exceeds pool, do you reject or queue?
[06:37] Maya: We expose routing policies: queue with backpressure, auto-scale (if Dedicated has burst capacity), or reject with graceful degrade to a cheaper model. For low-latency features we usually prefer reject-to-fallback rather than long queues.
[06:50] Emily: Ok. For the POC can you include quantization profiles? We want 13B int8 and float16 comparisons, and 70B q4/ptq-ish.
[06:59] Maya: Yes. We'll run quant profiles as part of the benchmark. We'll do 13B: f16 vs int8, and 70B: f16 vs q4xx (approx). Note quantized 70B still has significant tail variance.
[07:12] Samir: What telemetry will we get? We need token-level latency, per-route p95, per-token cost breakdown, and KV cache hit/miss rates.
[07:20] Jordan: Redwood Console exposes token-level breakdowns, per-route SLO dashboards, tracing at request level and KV metrics. We'll give you a demo link in the follow-up.
[07:29] Marcus: A practical question — for the 1.2s p95 streaming, what are typical failure modes we should watch for?
[07:35] Maya: Common issues: unbounded KV growth (memory pressure), long cold-starts when a model is not loaded, network spikes or throttling at the edge, and batching parameters set too large. We'll put guardrails into the POC.
[07:48] Emily: Can you also run a scenario where the KV store is persisted vs in-memory only? We think persistence will help with restarts.
[07:56] Maya: Yep we can compare in-memory vs persisted KV. Persistence adds a small read latency on cold reads but reduces memory footprint.
[08:05] Samir: Let's talk numbers again — you mentioned 1.2k tokens/sec to keep headroom for 200 sessions. If we 500 sessions what does that look like?
[08:13] Maya: Linear-ish but with multiplicative headroom. For 500 sessions at 1.7 tps = 850 tokens/sec baseline; with 3-4x headroom aim for 3.5k tps. That would need more GPUs: e.g., 13B path might need 5+ GPUs depending on exact tokens/sec per GPU in your quant profile. We'll get exact numbers from the benchmark.
[08:33] Samir: And for p95 measurement methodology — do you include network time to client?
[08:37] Jordan: We measure server-side generation p95 and client-side end-to-end p95 optionally. For your UX goal, we'll instrument end-to-end. We'll capture both.
[08:46] Emily: Any guidance on multiplexing sessions on a single GPU vs single-session-per-GPU? We want to avoid noisy neighbor problems.
[08:54] Maya: Multiplexing works if the model and batching are tuned. Dedicated pools give consistent performance; if you need extreme isolation you can pin sessions to nodes or reserve dedicated GPUs for critical customers.
[09:05] Marcus: On failover, how do you ensure ordering of streaming tokens when you route to fallback? We need summary continuity.
[09:12] Maya: We recommend client-side sequence tokens and server-side deterministic merging. Fallback will continue from last committed KV snapshot to preserve continuity. There's always a small risk of duplication but we provide idempotency keys.
[09:25] Samir: Ok good. I think we have enough to proceed to POC. Can we recap action items and next steps?
[09:30] Jordan: Sure. Quick recap: 1) Redwood to run token/sec benchmarks for 13B and 70B with quant profiles across 200/500/1000 concurrency; 2) Maya to produce p95 latency matrix and recommended pool sizing; 3) Jordan to send security pack (SOC2, KMS guide) and pricing spreadsheet; 4) schedule 24-48 hour POC in Dedicated EU region; 5) NexPath to provide sample prompt shapes and a small production trace for realistic load.
[09:52] Emily: We'll send the sample prompts and a one-day trace by end of day tomorrow.
[09:55] Marcus: We'll need SOW or pilot terms — can you include SLA/uptime in the pilot doc?
[09:59] Jordan: Yes we'll include pilot SOW and SLA targets.
[10:03] Samir: Timeline: If you can turn this POC and pricing in a week, we can decide within three weeks.
[10:08] Jordan: We'll aim for that. Anything else?
[10:11] Emily: One more, can we get an example dashboard or a short recording showing Console metrics for token breakdown?
[10:16] Maya: We'll attach a console screenshot and a short demo clip in the follow-up.
[10:20] Jordan: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the benchmark plan and calendar invites for the POC kickoff.
[10:27] Samir: Thanks, talk soon.
[10:30] Jordan: Bye all.

Notes on transcription: some domain terms may be slightly off, e.g., quant abbreviations and cloud instance names. There are short crosstalk sections and filler words left as-is to preserve authenticity.
